These users often install batteries to store excess solar generation during the day, which they can use during the evening or in the event of an outage. These “co-benefits” of BESS effectively lower the portion of the cost that customers would need to earn from bill savings in order to choose to adopt a BESS. However, these priorities can limit the extent to which batteries are used to respond to dynamic price signals, as they may be reserved for other functions. Especially important is the relationship between grid capacity constraints and outages during peak periods. When the grid is most strained—precisely when dynamic pricing is highest and price response is most needed—it is also at greater risk of experiencing an outage. During such critical events, customers who value reliability will likely hesitate to discharge their batteries for price response, instead conserving stored energy for backup purposes. This creates a tension between the grid’s need for load flexibility and the customer’s priority of maintaining power during outages. As a result, even though dynamic pricing may signal the need for battery discharge during peak demand, the likelihood of customer participation decreases during these high-risk periods. Lastly, there is a high correlation between adoption of behind-the-meter batteries and customers that have PV and are on net energy metering (NEM) rates. These customers may be disinclined to switch onto a dynamic rate, depending on the generation of NEM tariff they are on, as the dynamic rate is likely to offer them a lower value for their exported energy during hours of PV generation. Of course, presence of a BESS would limit some of this resistance, as it would allow 62 customers to instead discharge at the highest price hours, but it is possible that, regardless of the economics, these customers may have a certain inertia (including potentially having contracts with solar developers) that lead them to remain on their current rate that their system was designed for. Future dynamic tariff offerings should be closely compared to future NEM rate structures in order to assess the value proposition for customers installing solar PV with BESS in each case. This will inform the likelihood of those customers choosing a dynamic tariff, and therefore the quantity of behind-the-meter BESS that may be responding to dynamic rates. 4.5 Limitations and future work 4.5.1 Baseline load model One of the primary limitations of the current study is the reliance on a baseline load model developed from 2020-2021, which predominantly uses customer and meter data from 2019. Several significant shifts in electricity consumption patterns have occurred since then, limiting the accuracy of the model. For example, the model does not capture the substantial shifts in electricity demand patterns driven by the rise of remote work during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. With more people working from home, residential energy use has increased during what used to be off-peak hours, and commercial load profiles have changed as office buildings see reduced occupancy.
